analysis:
This batch has two documentation-only changes: a new changelog fragment (changelog.d/pipeline-decode-buffers.md) and an update to docs/architecture/hardware-support.md (a new paragraph at head lines 56-70, plus the date bump at line 3). No executable source is in the batch, so the code behind the described behavior (decode command buffers of up to 100 operations with no input-size bound, and request-charge pricing in QwenResidentPrefillTransient, Gemma4PrefillTransient and GPTOSSRequestStateBudget) was not reviewed.

Security-relevant claims in the docs:
- Per-request memory charges rise for the affected Qwen, Bonsai, Nemotron, Gemma 4 and GPT-OSS pairs. This is conservative for the admission and availability concerns, including T-016 and T-029.
- LOAD quotes and activation floors are unchanged, so the memory-cap invariants stay as documented.
- The docs admit that attention-kernel partials beyond the priced rows are not charged separately. That is a stated accounting gap, and it matters if larger command buffers push the real peak above the unchanged activation reserve. This is a memory-availability matter and does not touch the trust boundaries around consumer prompts, the provider keys or the attestation assets.
- The speed effect is unmeasured, and each family keeps the change only if a pair A/B shows a gain. No hardware qualification is claimed.
- Nothing in the batch touches the encrypted prefix cache (T-041), attestation, App Attest authorization, or the coordinator WebSocket protocol.

Open item for later review: the implementing Swift/cluster source and its tests (not in this batch) should confirm that the documented charge formula matches the code and that unbounded-input decode command buffers cannot exceed the process memory ledger. This is an integration question about the unreviewed implementation, not evidence of a regression, so no finding is raised.
